text_excerpt: When the chip fabrication plant broke ground outside Columbus two years ago, the headline number was 3,000 direct jobs. The harder number — finding 3,000 people qualified to do them — is now the region's defining challenge. The plant's first production lines need process technicians, most of whom require two-year degrees employers say local colleges barely offered until recently. In response, three community colleges built clean-room training labs in under a year, compressing what is normally a three-year program rollout. Enrollment exceeded projections by forty percent, but instructors remain scarce: anyone qualified to teach can earn double on the fab floor. Housing is the second bottleneck. Rents within twenty miles of the site have risen 28 percent since the announcement, and the 1,200-unit apartment complex meant to absorb workers is six months behind schedule. Local officials insist the growing pains are temporary and point to supplier announcements — eleven so far — as proof the bet is paying off. Skeptics note that two of those suppliers chose sites an hour away, where land is cheaper. The plant's general manager, Robert Chen, acknowledged the strain at a town hall last week but said the hiring timeline holds: first wafers by next summer, full staffing within eighteen months. Whether the training pipeline and the housing stock arrive on the same schedule is the question nobody at the town hall could answer with confidence. The water arithmetic adds another wrinkle few anticipated. Chip fabrication drinks millions of gallons daily, and while the plant funded a pipeline upgrade, farmers downstream watched creek levels all summer with growing unease. The utility's assurances — backed by a genuinely robust monitoring network — have mostly held, but one dry August tested everyone's nerves. On the training front, a bright spot: the first graduating class of 140 technicians placed at a 94 percent rate, most of them local residents earning more than their parents ever did. Instructor poaching continues, though, with the latest departure announced — awkwardly — during the town hall itself. The college president laughed it off, but the faculty lounge reportedly did not.
